cards.title: Track Margin Per Visitor (MPV) Instead of Revenue Per Visitor
cards.summary: Shift on-site reporting from revenue per visitor to margin per visitor so search and recommendation tuning chases profit, not just top-line sales.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your ecommerce analytics dashboard or setting goals for merchandising, search recommendations and paid traffic profitability.
steps: Pair each on-site revenue metric with its margin counterpart: alongside revenue per visitor, compute margin per visitor using product-level cost of goods for the specific items a visitor actually views and buys.

Calculate the margin contribution of a visitor, not just session value: subtract the cost of goods on the purchased basket from revenue, so a low-margin, high-support buyer is not counted as a strong customer.

Apply the same logic to customer segments: compare customer lifetime margin value rather than lifetime revenue, so a regular buyer of low-margin high-price items (the source's example: ten $5,000 laptops bought at thin margin with heavy support cost) can be recognized as potentially unprofitable next to a buyer of many high-margin small items (e.g. staplers at strong margin).

Feed the margin signal into search and recommendation goals: instruct AI tooling to weight private-label and high-margin items higher on results and listing pages where relevance is comparable, instead of ranking purely on popularity.

Review margin trajectory, not just one month: the source's position is that retailer margins are compressing (around six percent today trending toward roughly two percent in the source's 2024-2025 forecast, with some large sellers losing money), so treat shrinking MPV as a strategic planning input.
Reinvest the profit captured: lower acquisition cost per margin dollar lets you bid and spend more on traffic that remains profitable.
caveats: MPV depends on accurate per-SKU cost of goods, which many catalogs lack; treat the metric as directionally useful until COGS data is clean.
The presenter (Coveo) argues promotions and private labels should get extra visibility; this is a source opinion about business-goal-weighted ranking, not a universal rule.
The claimed 72 percent margin boost for one customer is a case example, not a benchmark you can assume.

cards.title: Partner for Search and AI Instead of Building In-House
cards.summary: Treat search, recommendations and merchandising AI as buy-or-partner capabilities so your team spends its time on brand and customer strategy, not infrastructure.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build or buy the search, recommendation and personalization stack on your storefront.
steps: Separate what differentiates you from what is commodity technology: brand promise, assortment, layouts, supplier and persona decisions are yours; ranking algorithms, query understanding and data normalization are the sort of capability specialist vendors already solve at scale.

Weigh the talent reality before committing to build: the source's argument is that retailers cannot reliably out-compete major tech firms for top engineering talent, so proprietary build programs tend to stall.

Consider ownership cost honestly: an executive at a gifting company in the source describes spending so much P&L running self-built technical infrastructure that the team lost mindshare for differentiating the brand.

Choose partners for track record across many clients rather than one-off custom builds, and require them to expose the business objectives you are optimizing (e.g. margin, relevance, private-label push).
Free up internal merchandisers from manual term monitoring and layout policing; have them set strategy and let the tool automate predictive tuning.
Confirm the current integration options, data requirements and reporting interfaces directly with the vendor, since product capabilities and storefront integrations change.
caveats: Attributed to a Coveo executive who sells search and recommendation technology; the build-vs-buy conclusion is their commercial position as well as their experience.
Some businesses with genuinely unusual catalogs or regulatory constraints may still need custom work; verify fit before adopting a standard vendor solution.

cards.title: Make B2B Buying Experiences Match Consumer Standards
cards.summary: Apply the same low-friction search, discovery and self-service standards to B2B storefronts that professional buyers already expect from consumer sites.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing a B2B or wholesale storefront's search, documentation and self-service ordering flow.
steps: Assume the buyer is also a consumer: the source's point is that professional buyers bring Amazon-and-Google-trained expectations into work purchases, so evaluate your B2B site against the leading B2C experiences you personally use.

Support long, complex consideration: the source describes B2B orders with around 70 line items and average order values near $500,000, with buyers touching content, specifications, supporting documentation and search across five to ten or more touch points before committing.

Attach the supporting content to the buying path: technical documentation, compliance information and specification detail should be discoverable in the same search and product flow as the item itself, not buried elsewhere.

Prioritize self-service over forcing contact: the source states most professional buyers do not want to call a sales rep, and search failures push them into costly phone calls or customer service contacts.

Test with the intent that a poor discovery experience signals incompetence to a B2B buyer: if the buyer cannot find what they need, they may conclude you cannot serve their organization at all, not just that they cannot find one item.
Reduce login and page-thumbing friction; the source reports buyers abandon experiences that repeatedly log them out or make them page through many screens.
caveats: Order-value and touchpoint figures come from the source's own clients and are illustrative, not universal B2B benchmarks.
Some B2B purchasing is contractually or procedurally locked into procurement systems; the consumer-grade expectation applies to the portion of the flow you actually control.

cards.title: Use Predictive, Intent-Based Ranking Over Popularity Ranking
cards.summary: Replace popularity-only ranking in search and recommendations with intent signals and explicit business goals so results fit both the shopper and your margin.
cards.use_when: Configuring search result ranking, listing-page sort order or product recommendation widgets on your storefront.
steps: Combine explicit and implicit signals: use queries and typed intent alongside behavioral signals such as what the visitor has previously purchased, viewed and navigated toward.

Move beyond popularity because popularity ignores the individual: the source notes a best-selling item may not fit that shopper's size, need or context, and popularity does not reflect the business's goals.

Feed business goals into the ranking layer: private-label products, higher-margin items or manufacturer-promoted products can be given extra visibility on results and listing pages where relevance allows.

Handle ambiguous queries with contextual signals: the source's example is a sporting goods search where typing 'BO' could mean boating, hunting or general footwear; context such as the section a shopper is browsing should disambiguate.

Design cross-category suggestion logic where it fits household or fleet purchasing: the source cites a footwear retailer where showing men's and kids' shoes alongside women's shoes raised order value, and a fleet-parts supplier that recommends companion replacement parts to get trucks back on the road faster.
Treat the engine as probabilistic: the source frames AI ranking as 'being less wrong' and improving as it learns from outcomes, so monitor and correct rather than trusting it blindly.
caveats: Requires sufficient behavioral and product data; thin catalogs or new stores may not have enough signal for intent-based ranking to outperform simple rules.
The footwear and fleet-parts examples are the source's client anecdotes, not validated benchmarks.
Relevance must remain the constraint; ranking purely by margin will damage trust and conversion.

cards.title: Design for Digital Distraction and Zero-Friction Interfaces
cards.summary: Assume buyers are interrupted mid-task and remove every avoidable step so a partially completed session can still convert.
cards.use_when: Reviewing cart, checkout, account and browsing flows for friction that loses distracted shoppers.
steps: Plan for interruption: the source cites research that customers face roughly 1,400 digital interactions a day today, projected toward 5,000 by 2025, which means sessions start and stop mid-purchase.
Reduce steps to the minimum: the source contrasts modern expectations with legacy B2B workflows built on mainframes and multi-screen order entry, arguing buyers no longer have patience for it.
Cut context loss: avoid designs that require repeated logins or force shoppers through many pages before they can find or buy the item.
Recognize that a search miss has a direct cost: if the item is on page two or three, the result is often an abandoned session, a phone call or a service contact instead of a purchase.

Anticipate rather than interrogate: show likely next items, companion products and relevant options so a buyer without a complete shopping list can assemble one, which the source frames as making it easier to give you money.
Treat any unattended digital surface as a 24/7 commitment: the source's framing is that brands must deliver a strong experience at all hours, not only during business hours.
caveats: The 1,400-to-5,000 interactions-per-day figures come from cited vendor research and are directional, not a measurement standard.
Some B2B or regulated flows legitimately require extra steps; remove friction deliberately rather than indiscriminately.

cards.title: Personalize Discoveries That Shorten Time-to-Satisfaction
cards.summary: Use known history and signals to surface better-fit products so buyers reach satisfaction faster and remember the brand afterward.
cards.use_when: Setting up personalization rules, homepage or landing-page personalization and recommendation blocks on your storefront.
steps: Use history as a discovery aid: the source describes personalization that uses prior purchases, viewed items and navigation to land a visitor on a better-fit product rather than a generic result.
Target a shorter path to satisfaction: recognized shoppers spend less time searching, and the source links that reduction to stronger loyalty and brand affinity.

Aim for memorability because commoditization is one click away: the source's argument is that if customers cannot remember where they bought something, the experience was ordinary and you are at risk of being replaced by a marketplace that remembers them.
Test personalization against seasonality and new items: the source notes the tension between what you know from past purchases and continuous experimentation as seasons and assortments change.
Combine personalization with rank-level goals (margin, private label) so the tailored experience also serves the business, rather than only showing the familiar product again.
caveats: Personalization can narrow assortment exposure; monitor whether strict history-based surfacing hides new or discovery items.
The loyalty and memorability claims are the source's reasoning rather than measured outcomes.

cards.title: Set a Concrete Business Objective Before Applying AI
cards.summary: Define the business goal and the signals the model should listen to before deploying any search, recommendation or merchandising AI.
cards.use_when: Scoping an AI or machine-learning project for search, recommendations, merchandising or pricing on your storefront.
steps: Write the objective in business terms first: the source's warning is that 'AI for AI's sake' produces technology that does nothing measurable and shows up mainly in investor decks.
Decide which signals the system may use — prior purchases, viewing and navigation behavior, query terms, seasonality, margin data — and which it must ignore.
Define the outcome metric in advance: margin per visitor, conversion, order value or another specific measure you will judge the deployment by.
Match the technology to the objective: recommendation engines tuned for margin will rank differently from engines tuned purely for relevance or popularity.

Shift merchandiser time from manual monitoring to strategy: stop hand-checking which terms return nothing and policing layouts; set the business objectives, personas and assortment direction the engine should serve.
Accept that the engine guesses and learns: monitor and correct errors rather than treating rankings as fixed rules.
caveats: Requires a data and instrumentation baseline; objectives cannot be optimized if the signals are not captured.
The source is a vendor advocate of AI merchandising, so treat their framing of effortless gains with appropriate skepticism and validate with a controlled test.

cards.title: Measure Profit Trajectory and Customer Margin Value Continuously
cards.summary: Review margin trajectory and per-customer profitability trends, not single-period revenue, when planning assortment and acquisition spend.
cards.use_when: Running quarterly or monthly ecommerce performance reviews that inform assortment, pricing and traffic investment decisions.
steps: Track the trajectory, not the snapshot: the source urges retailers to watch the direction of margins and profitability over time rather than only current revenue growth.
Compare customer segments on margin, not gross spend: contrast a high-revenue, low-margin buyer who consumes support cost against a modest-revenue, high-margin repeat buyer.

Treat acquisition spend as a function of margin: because cost, supply chain and energy inflation raise cost of goods while purchasing power falls, the source's logic is that profitable margin per visitor determines how much you can afford to bid for traffic.

Watch for growth-at-all-costs traps: the source notes some sellers above a billion in revenue knowingly lose money to defend market share, and frames that as a strategic choice with a cost, not a default.
Account for support and service cost in the customer value calculation so negative-margin customers are visible rather than hidden inside revenue totals.
caveats: The source's margin percentages (about six percent now trending to roughly two percent) are its own forecast and should be replaced with your actual figures.
Customer-level margin accounting requires cost allocation choices; state your method and keep it consistent over time.

input.source_name: Customer Digital Experience is Key to Successful Ecommerce.docx
input.text:
05-SET / store setup and tech Goes here. A strategic discussion on leveraging AI-powered search, recommendation engines, and personalization to optimize both B2B and B2C e-commerce customer experiences (CX). Covers the "build vs. buy" technology dilemma and the shift from tracking top-line revenue to optimizing for margin per visitor. Not here. • Traffic generation or paid media advertising -> 06-MEA • Physical product sourcing, 3PL, and freight -> 18-COG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Explains how integrating third-party AI search and discovery tools improves conversion rates, customer retention, and overall profitability without the overhead of building proprietary tech. modules: [SET] topics: [e-commerce tech, customer experience, AI search, personalization, B2B e-commerce, margin per visitor, conversion rate optimization, build vs. buy] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. B2B consumerization / how professional B2B buyers now expect the same frictionless, predictive, Amazon-like search and discovery experiences they receive as everyday consumers; digital distraction / addressing the reality that consumers face 1,400 to 5,000 digital interactions daily, necessitating zero-friction e-commerce interfaces; build vs. buy / arguing against building proprietary search and AI technology in-house, recommending instead that brands partner with specialized vendors to free up internal teams for strategic merchandising; AI in merchandising / utilizing machine learning not just to show "popular" items, but to dynamically recommend products based on user intent and specific business goals (e.g., pushing high-margin private labels); profitability metrics / shifting focus from "growth at all costs" and traditional Revenue Per Visitor to Margin Per Visitor (MPV) to combat shrinking retail profit margins.

Look for.

Margin Per Visitor (MPV): The strategic shift from tracking Revenue Per Visitor to tracking the actual net margin of the items a specific user is buying, using AI recommendation engines to push higher-margin products.

The "Build vs. Buy" Fallacy: The argument that e-commerce brands should not act like software companies by trying to build their own search/AI tools, as they cannot effectively compete for top engineering talent against major tech firms.

B2B Consumerization: The trend where professional B2B buyers (who may be placing complex, 70-item, $500k orders) now demand the exact same seamless search experience they get on major B2C platforms.

Intent-Based Merchandising: Moving away from analog merchandising (simply showing what is "popular") to predictive AI that tailors recommendations to individual user intent and basket combinations.

Skip. The podcast host's introductory banter, the guest's career background at Deloitte, and the explicit promotional pitches for Coveo and the SAP store link.

Scope mix. 30% baseline (general customer experience principles), 70% growth (AI tech integration and advanced profitability metrics). Volume. ~350 words.
